newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Iraq seeks French wheat with oil revenue.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Iraq seeks French wheat with oil revenue.

text.p: French firms are lining up deals to sell wheat to Iraq as Baghdad prepares to export oil for the first time in six years, grain traders said on Thursday.
Talks have started on an Iraqi tender to buy 100,000 tonnes of French wheat, and could lead to more purchases to help meet Iraq's need for two million tonnes of commodities, they said.
"All we need to know is whether they are going to buy 100,000 tonnes, 500,000 tonnes or a million," a source in Paris close to the negotiations said.
Grain prices have risen this week, partly on speculation that Iraq would buy wheat with its oil money under a U.N. initiative allowing it to export limited amounts of crude.
The oil sale will allow it buy food and medicine needed to provide relief to ordinary Iraqis hit by sanctions imposed for President Saddam Hussein's invasion of Kuwait in August 1990.
Hopes of Russian buying and news that India would import for the first time in four years pushed wheat prices higher again on Thursday as Iraq negotiated the purchase.
Iraq, proclaiming victory over Washington, inaugurated its first oil flow through Turkey on Tuesday since sanctions began.
Turkish news agency Anatolia said on Thursday tankers would be able to start loading the oil at a Turkish port the next day, allowing Baghdad to start buying the supplies it needed.
If sold, traders said the French wheat would reach Iraq in two equal shipments of 50,000 tonnes in January and February. Such a deal would be worth around $15 million at today's prices.
But banking sources in Paris said several commodity firms had complained of bureaucracy in the oil-for-food arrangements set up by the U.N., and wanted laxer rules.
Iraq is allowed to sell enough oil to raise $2 billion in renewable six-month stages under strict U.N. supervision, while the wider economic sanctions will continue to apply.
About half the money raised will be deducted for U.N. costs, reparations and a special relief programme for northern Kurds.
Iraq's Minister of Trade Mohammed Mehdi Saleh said on Sunday that wheat was the main component of two million tonnes of goods Baghdad intended to buy when the oil started flowing.
France, which has lent conditional support to Iraq's calls for a complete halt to economic sanctions, is expected to be among the first to benefit from oil and grain deals.
French oil giants Elf Aquitaine and Total SA have said they are interested in buying Iraqi crude and French grain firms have already made contact with Baghdad.
France is Europe's largest wheat exporter and producer.
Exporters are looking for business after a global crop recovery caused prices to collapse from records seen in April.
Iraq's main supplier before sanctions started in August 1990 was Australia, followed by the U.S., Canada and France.

Benchmark U.S. wheat prices, which set the direction for France, regained a psychological level of $4.00 a bushel (about $150 a tonne) on Thursday after falling as low as $3.62 a bushel last month. April's record was $7.50 a bushel.
India, which has enjoyed surpluses after a drive to boost self-sufficiency, said on Thursday it would import two million tonnes this financial year to stop its own food prices rising.
Traders said that after a disappointing harvest Russia may soon compete with Iraq, India, Egypt and others to buy wheat. But there were major doubts over Moscow's ability to pay.
